analysis.one_liner: Bars federal fracking rules on federal land in states that have their own rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 235-187 on November 20, 2013, but the Senate never voted, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the Interior Department from enforcing any federal hydraulic fracturing rules on federal land in any state that has its own fracking rules. The Department would have to defer to state rules for everything related to fracking on federal land, even when those rules are weaker, different, or do not meet federal guidelines. It would also add peer-review requirements to an EPA study of fracking's effects on drinking water and require an annual report on state fracking activities.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land, which would avoid a single federal standard for fracking on those lands and instead face whatever each state chooses to require, with no minimum federal floor for well construction, testing, or chemical disclosure.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars Interior from enforcing any federal fracking regulation, guidance, or permit requirement in states that have their own fracking rules [S2].

It requires Interior to defer to state rules for all fracking activities on federal land regardless of whether those rules are duplicative, more or less restrictive, have different requirements, or do not meet federal guidelines [S2].
It would let federal fracking go forward under each state's own permitting system, with states submitting their rules to the Bureau of Land Management and the Secretary making them public [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People who live near or use water downstream of fracking on federal land would lose a federal baseline for the process, since federal rules could not apply wherever a state has any fracking rules. Federal land is owned by all taxpayers, so the public that owns the minerals would rely entirely on each state's choices for oversight and chemical disclosure.

drawbacks.text: The deference to states applies even when state rules are less restrictive or do not meet federal guidelines, so there is no federal minimum standard for fracking on federal land in any state that has rules of its own [S2].

Chemical disclosure would depend entirely on what each state requires, since the bill only requires states to submit copies of any chemical-disclosure rules they already have and makes no disclosure mandatory [S4].

An amendment offered by Rep. Rush Holt to preserve federal and state authority to require public disclosure of fracking chemicals was rejected in the Committee of the Whole [S6], and a motion to recommit with similar instructions failed 188-232 [S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued that states have long regulated oil and gas and that this prevents duplicative or conflicting federal and state permitting for the same wells on federal land. The cost is that federal land belongs to all Americans, and under this bill there would be no federal floor: a state could have weak or minimal fracking rules and the Interior Department would still have to defer to them, including on chemical disclosure that residents near the wells would otherwise be able to demand from the federal government. The EPA drinking-water study would also face added peer-review requirements and a fixed release deadline of September 30, 2016 [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 235-187, was read twice in the Senate and placed on the calendar, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 18, 2013, and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which ordered it reported amended 23-15 on July 31 [S6].
The House passed it 235-187 on November 20, 2013: 223 of 231 voting Republicans voted yes and 12 of 200 voting Democrats did [S8].

A motion to recommit with instructions to preserve the authority of Interior and the states to require public disclosure of fracking chemicals failed 188-232, with 223 of 230 voting Republicans voting no [S7].
The Senate received the bill November 21, 2013, read it twice and placed it on the calendar on December 9, but no vote ever occurred before the 113th Congress ended [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land kept operating under state rules alone for the rest of the Congress, with no federal fracking standard either blocked or created. The public was spared the bill's prohibition on federal enforcement because it never became law.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party: 223 of 231 voting Republicans yes versus 12 of 200 voting Democrats, and the motion to recommit failed 188-232 with 223 of 230 voting Republicans opposed [S8] [S7].

industries.note: The bill would have removed federal fracking standards on federal land wherever a state had its own rules, including rules weaker than federal guidelines, leaving drillers to answer only to state regulators. The public owns the federal minerals and the groundwater near them, so weaker oversight of drilling on that land shifts risk onto people who live nearby.

The bill would have made state rules the only binding rules for fracking on federal land, formally entrenching state primacy regardless of stringency. Some states run rigorous programs; the bill treats them all identically.
